title: The death of a scammer Tonggo Simangunsong
content:
Poipet, near the Thailand–Cambodia border. Credit: wattana / Shutterstock.com




I

t was the end of 2024. Almost five months after losing his job at a food and beverage company, thirty-nine-year-old Rasdy Fawzi told his wife, Kiki Tresia Ginting, that he was going to accept a job in Cambodia.




Kiki was concerned, and for good reason. The man who’d offered him the job was part of a scam syndicate; the recruitment agency was unregistered and the work Fawzi would be undertaking was illegal. She’d heard stories of young Indonesians trapped in Cambodia, tortured and forced to work as scammers.




“I worried and asked my husband about his safety if he worked there, but he said, ‘That’s okay, it’s fine, don’t worry’,” she recalls. Fawzi reassured her many times that his friend had been there, too, and he trusted him. He believed that he was too old for any company in Indonesia to want to hire him for the same role he’d had in mobile sales marketing with his previous employer. While going to Cambodia was risky, the salary offered would be more than enough to support their small family. It was an opportunity he didn’t want to pass up. In the end, there was nothing Kiki could do but let him go and pray for his safety.

title: When the tigers become rats Jake Adelstein
content:
Yakuza fan magazines like Jitsuwa Document were sold all over Japan until as late as 2018. Credit: Jake Adelstein




Yakuza: A 400-Year History of the Japanese Underworld




Andrew Rankin




Basic Books: 2026




.




E

very few years, someone announces that the Japanese organised crime groups known as the yakuza are finished. Every few years, a book tries to explain what, exactly, has been dying.




Many people still assume “the yakuza” are one monolithic criminal organisation ruling Japan from the shadows. That’s completely wrong. They are more than twenty separate criminal organisations. And they have never lived in the shadows.




Andrew Rankin has probably written the best explanation yet of their unusual character:




Japanese underworld analysts tend to regard the yakuza as a uniquely Japanese phenomenon, and so they dislike the term Japanese mafia. Criminologists in the West have defined a mafia as an organized crime group that specializes in protection: A mafia supplies and sells protection and aggressively tries to monopolize the supply of protection within specific fields of business, both legal and illegal. Understood in that way, the yakuza groups surely constitute a Japanese variety of mafia. title: Chronicler of insurgencies Kristian Odebjer
content:
Credit: Apirak Kosakijjawut




I

n October 1985, the Swedish writer Bertil Lintner, then thirty-two, crossed illegally from Indian Nagaland into Burma. A year-and-a-half later, he emerged in Xishuangbanna in Yunnan, China. He’d trekked with his wife, Hseng Noung Lintner, and infant daughter along 2,000 kilometres of Burmese jungle paths, crossing the Chindwin, Mali Hka, and Salween rivers. The aim of the journey was to report on little-known insurgency campaigns waged by groups like the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and the Communist Party of Burma (CPB).




This was journalism undertaken by a writer prepared to immerse himself fully in order to tell an important story. The risks were real: on occasion, the family found themselves caught in the middle of active combat. Lintner’s reporting from the trail appeared in the 

Far Eastern Economic Review

, a weekly news magazine. Published in English in 1990, the book 

Land of Jade: A Journey from India through Northern Burma to China

—part travel diary, part eyewitness account—told the story of Burma’s ethnic conflicts through Lintner’s writing and Hseng Noung’s photographs.

author: Mekong Review 2
title: The ineligibles Thammika Songkaeo
content:
BTS at the 61st Annual Grammy Awards in 2019. Credit: Kathy Hutchins / Shutterstock.com




W

hen BTS, the K-pop boyband, refused to submit their music for consideration in the 2026 Grammy Awards, artists worldwide were filled with pride but also envy. Many know that to walk away from the table, one must first be invited to sit down. For artists outside the West, the Grammys, the Oscars, and major literary prizes represent something far more coercive than mere vanity.




Art requires no institutional seal to be profound. The best art in the world is likely unknown to the mainstream. In late capitalism, however, discoverability has come to be a major factor in dictating an artist’s success. While BTS has enough clout to turn down the Grammys, many artists—operating in domestic ecosystems that lack the infrastructure for global marketing and distribution—know that major prizes do not merely recognise creative excellence but also manufacture further success: for instance, foreign-rights advances, festival marquee placement, and prime spots in retail outlets.




BTS has been nominated at the Grammys before, but has never won. title: Chasing the burning pearl Angela Sim
content:
The fire dragon in flight. Credit: Yeo G.T.




I

n the pantheon of Chinese mythology, few symbols command as much awe as the dragon (龍). Majestic and unrestrained, it stands as the preeminent member of the four divine creatures, alongside the turtle (龟), phoenix (凤), and qilin (麒麟). Historically, the dragon was the ultimate emblem of the Son of Heaven. During the Ming dynasty, the five-clawed dragon adorned the 

buzi

 (補子), or rank badges, of the Emperor’s robes. These intricate badges weren’t merely decorative; they were markers of nobility and merit, awarded to those who performed exceptional service.




Despite its omnipresence, the dragon remains a creature of pure myth, never witnessed by the human eye yet vividly rendered through the ages. It is a biological mosaic; a lion’s nose and tiger’s mouth paired with the ears of an ox and the shimmering eyes of a goldfish. Crowned with deer antlers and grounded by eagle claws, its energetic, snake-like body is shielded by the underbelly of a clam. To the Chinese world, this auspicious creature is more than legend; it is spiritual sustenance used to conquer nature and ward off evil. Whether dwelling in the depths of the water or the vastness of the sky, the dragon’s eleven distinct forms remain a powerful symbol of protection.

title: The state and the sin Rafly Gilang Pratama
content:
Calling themselves “boti hunters”, young men on motorcycles ride through dark alleys in Bogor targeting people they perceive to be queer. Credit: Dominic Kurniawan Suryaputra / Unsplash




T

he young men in the videos sounded as though they were having fun.




It was well past midnight in Bogor, Indonesia’s “rain city”. The roads were mostly empty and the boys rode motorcycles, looking for people they perceived to be gay, effeminate, or transgender. They revved their engines as they rode through the streets, shouting: “Bersih-bersih boti!”




“Clean up the boti!”




They proudly called themselves “boti hunters”, turning 

boti

, a slang term derived from ‘bottom’, into the name of their little vigilante enterprise. There’s something accidentally homoerotic about groups of young men spending their midnight hours patrolling pitch-black alleys thinking about nothing but bottoms—but then someone in the frame starts running for their life, and the joke dies.




Accounts carrying variations of the “boti hunter” name soon appeared online. In the videos, the boys laugh and shout while they chase people through the streets, filming everything for a little bit of social media clout.




I’ve heard those laughs before.

pesantren

, an Islamic boarding school, in West Java. I entered primary school through a scholarship programme for
